[Post: 26M | How much percentage of my salary should I ideally have SIPs ?] I wouldn’t say your decision was necessarily wrong, but I would definitely pause the ₹1.6L SIP before doing anything else. Your biggest issue is not SIP percentage. You have a potentially large house requirement sitting in the background, yet most of the ₹12L has now moved into market linked assets. A generic recommendation based only on your salary and expenses can look perfectly logical while being completely unsuitable once the house timeline is included. Also, selling overlapping funds after a year purely because someone told you they are overlapping is not automatically good advice. There can be tax, exit load, market timing and portfolio construction implications. Equity MF redemption is generally fairly quick, but quick access does not mean the money is safe. If the market drops 20% just when your property paperwork gets cleared, you could be forced to sell at exactly the wrong time. This is one of those cases where I would separate the house corpus, emergency money and long term wealth corpus first , and only then decide the SIP. The ₹1.6L number may turn out to be perfectly sensible, or completely wrong, depending on that calculation. Your situation is actually detailed enough that I would not rely on a generic online allocation without doing the full numbers properly.

Just keep these basic points in mind: 1) Buy a pure pure term plan. No riders. No return of premium. No add-ons. No endowment plan, no nothing. 2) Go for a coverage as high as you can afford, considering you are young and premiums will be lower. Premium increases with age for the same coverage amount. Obviously, keep the sum assured within 15-20x of your annual income. Revisit this a few years later when there is a significant change in your life status (marriage / more dependents / increased income). One policy will not be sufficient for your entire life. eg. Even if you take a 5 Cr policy now, as per your current income and expenses, it will be nowhere close to enough 25 years down the line, when you are at the peak of your career, earning big bucks, with maybe a couple of large EMIs, and having kids heading into college. Of course, inflation will make 5 crore value closer to 1-1.5 crore over 25 years. So it won't be enough anyways. 3) Don't go for limited premium paying period. You might go for monthly payment if you want to minimise the large-ish one time annual outgo. 4) Don't go for the cheapest one you find on policybazaar or any aggregator site. Pick an insurer from the top 4-5 (HDFC Life, ICICI Pru, etc). You don't need an agent to "help" you. Most of them just try to upsell you into something else. 5) Take life cover till age 60-62 only. Life insurance is only to protect your dependents against loss of your income. Unless you plan to keep working beyond 60, you don't need insurance beyond that age. Insurance is not meant to be an inheritance for your dependents.

This strategy is highly unrealistic, severely flawed, and extremely dangerous for an average retail investor. The video blends basic passive investing with high-risk derivatives trading, presenting it as a simple "hack." Here is a practical reality check on why this strategy falls apart in the real world: 1. The Math is Borderline Impossible (47% CAGR) To turn ₹5,000 a month into ₹1 Crore in exactly 10 years, you need an annualized return (CAGR) of ~47% every single year. * For context, the Nifty 50 averages about 12-14%. * Warren Buffett, one of the greatest investors in history, has a lifetime average of about 20-22%. * Expecting an average retail investor to consistently generate a 47% return over a decade is a financial fantasy. 2. The "Buy on Dips" SIP is Inefficient (Cash Drag) The video suggests holding your daily ₹1,000 allocation on "green" days and only investing on "red" days. * The Reality: Stock markets generally go up more often than they go down. If the market is positive for two weeks, your cash sits idle in a bank account earning almost nothing. This is called "cash drag." * Decades of financial research show that "Time in the market beats timing the market." A disciplined, automated monthly SIP almost always outperforms a manual strategy because you don't miss out on sudden compounding rallies while waiting for a dip. Plus, logging in every day at 3:15 PM turns passive wealth generation into a stressful daily chore. 3. Mutual Funds vs. ETFs: Half the Truth The video villainizes Mutual Funds for Expense Ratios and Exit Loads to push ETFs. * The Reality: You can buy Direct Index Mutual Funds which have expense ratios nearly identical to ETFs (around 0.1% to 0.2%). * The Hidden Costs of ETFs: While ETFs don't have exit loads, you have to pay brokerage fees, DP charges, and STT every time you buy or sell. Furthermore, many ETFs in India suffer from low liquidity, meaning the price you buy at (Ask) and the price you sell at (Bid) can have a wide gap, immediately erasing any savings you made on the expense ratio. 4. Pledging for Intraday Trading is a Trap This is the most dangerous part of the strategy. The creator suggests pledging your long-term ETFs to get margin for algorithmic intraday trading to make an extra "3% a month" (36% a year). * The Margin Illusion: Margin is a loan. If your automated intraday trade hits a stop-loss (which it will, frequently), that loss must be settled in cash at the end of the day. * The Liquidation Risk: If you don't have spare cash lying around to cover your trading losses, your broker will automatically forcefully sell your pledged long-term ETFs to recover the money. Your retirement portfolio will be wiped out to pay for your day-trading losses. * The Success Rate: SEBI's official reports state that 9 out of 10 retail traders lose money in intraday and F&O trading. Earning a consistent 3% a month strictly through intraday trading is exceptionally difficult, even for Wall Street professionals. The Verdict The creator is effectively taking a safe, boring, and highly successful strategy (passive SIPs) and using it as bait to funnel viewers into algorithmic intraday trading (where brokers and software providers make massive commissions). If you want to build wealth safely without turning it into a full-time job: stick to a simple, automated monthly SIP in a Direct Nifty 50 Mutual Fund, increase the amount by 10% every year as your salary grows, and ignore daily market fluctuations.

Good educational effort, but I strongly disagree with some points in this strategy. 1. Expense Ratio A 2% expense ratio does NOT mean ₹1 lakh invested today becomes ₹98,000 immediately. Expenses are reflected proportionately in the NAV over time. 2. Exit Load Exit load is also not a permanent cost. Many equity funds commonly have around 1% exit load if redeemed within 12 months, depending on the scheme. 3. ETF vs Active Mutual Fund ETF/index investing is cheaper because it follows a predefined index. An active fund charges more for research, company selection, portfolio changes and continuous monitoring. That additional 0.30–1% cost should therefore be compared with the actual alpha and risk management delivered after expenses, not looked at only as a cost. 4. “Wait for a market fall and buy the dip” sounds easy, but practically it is market timing. Nobody knows whether a 5% fall is the bottom or whether another 15% fall is coming. Time in the market is generally more important than trying to perfectly time the market. 5. Pledging investments and using that money for intraday trading adds another layer of risk. There are brokerage, financing/interest costs, taxes and other charges. Leverage can multiply losses just as quickly as profits. Showing a theoretical 30–40% return is easy; consistently generating it in the real market is completely different. 6. There is also an important conflict-of-interest question. Upstox currently charges up to ₹20 per executed intraday order, and its Authorised Person model can include sharing of brokerage generated by referred clients. So if someone recommending frequent intraday trading also earns directly or indirectly from the brokerage generated, that commercial relationship should be clearly disclosed to viewers. The issue isn't whetherb someone earns ₹5, ₹10 or another amount per trade. The important point is that more trading can mean more brokerage revenue, while the investor carries the trading risk. My simple view: Your profession/business should generate your cash flow. Your investments should compound that wealth. You don't need to turn investing into another full-time profession. ETFs have their place. Active mutual funds have their place. Professional advisors have their place. But high-frequency trading, leverage and trying to catch every market dip should never be presented as an easy route to wealth creation. Invest consistently. Stay invested. Focus on your own expertise and let investment professionals do the work they are trained to do.
